title: Building HTTP Services & Middleware
summary: Go's `net/http` is a complete, production-grade HTTP server in the standard library. The whole design rests on one tiny interface — `http.Handler` — and one composition pattern: **middleware**, a function that wraps a handler to add cross-cutting behavior (logging, auth, recovery, timeouts). Master the Handler/ServeMux/middleware trio and you can build clean, observable, resilient services with no framework.

subtopics.title: The http.Handler interface
subtopics.explanation: Everything that serves HTTP implements one method: ServeHTTP(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request). The server runs each request in its own goroutine and calls ServeHTTP. Because it's a single-method interface, handlers compose trivially.

subtopics.title: HandlerFunc: functions as handlers
subtopics.explanation: http.HandlerFunc is an adapter type: a func(w, r) with a ServeHTTP method that just calls itself. It lets you use a plain function anywhere a Handler is expected, which is why so much Go HTTP code is just functions.

subtopics.title: Routing with ServeMux
subtopics.explanation: ServeMux maps URL patterns to handlers. Since Go 1.22 the standard mux supports methods and path wildcards (e.g. "GET /users/{id}"), so you often don't need a third-party router. It returns 404/405 automatically for unmatched routes/methods.

subtopics.title: Middleware as handler-wrapping
subtopics.explanation: Middleware is a function `func(http.Handler) http.Handler`: it takes the next handler and returns a new one that runs code before and/or after calling next.ServeHTTP. Chaining them composes cross-cutting concerns (logging -> recovery -> auth -> handler) cleanly.

subtopics.title: Per-request context
subtopics.explanation: Each *http.Request carries a context.Context (r.Context()) that is cancelled when the client disconnects or the server times out. Middleware attaches request-scoped values (request ID, authenticated user) via context, and handlers pass r.Context() into downstream DB/RPC calls so cancellation propagates.
subtopics.example: ctx := context.WithValue(r.Context(), userKey, u); next.ServeHTTP(w, r.WithContext(ctx))

subtopics.title: Timeouts & graceful shutdown
subtopics.explanation: A naked http.Server has no timeouts — one slow client can pin a connection. Set ReadTimeout/WriteTimeout/IdleTimeout, and on SIGTERM call srv.Shutdown(ctx) to stop accepting new connections and let in-flight requests finish within a deadline.

foundations.overview: You can build a real HTTP service in Go with nothing but the standard library, because net/http already includes the server, routing, and a clean extension model. The key insight is that an entire web service is just an http.Handler — and middleware is how you layer logging, authentication, panic recovery, and timeouts around it without touching business logic. Once the Handler/HandlerFunc/middleware pattern clicks, frameworks become optional.
foundations.formalDefinition: An http.Handler is any value with a ServeHTTP(ResponseWriter, *Request) method. An http.Server runs an accept loop, spawns a goroutine per connection, and dispatches each request through a ServeMux to the matching Handler. Middleware is a Handler-to-Handler decorator that adds behavior around ServeHTTP.
foundations.whyItMatters: HTTP services are the backbone of backend systems, and Go's net/http powers a huge share of cloud infrastructure (Docker, Kubernetes, Prometheus). Knowing the Handler/middleware model lets you build clean, testable, resilient services — and explaining it well is a staple of backend interviews.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of middleware as airport security layers wrapping a gate (your handler). A passenger (request) passes through ID check (logging), the metal detector (auth), and a safety net (panic recovery) on the way in; some checks also inspect them on the way out (response logging). Each layer can let them through, modify them, or turn them back early.
foundations.runtimePerspective: http.Server's Serve loop accepts connections and starts a goroutine per connection (which handles its requests sequentially for HTTP/1.1, concurrently via streams for HTTP/2). Each request's r.Context() is cancelled when the client disconnects or a configured timeout fires, so handlers that pass it downstream stop wasted work automatically.
foundations.realWorldUsage: REST/JSON APIs, internal microservices, health and metrics endpoints, webhooks, reverse proxies — virtually every Go backend exposes an net/http server, often with a thin middleware stack.
foundations.businessImpact: A correctly configured server (timeouts, graceful shutdown, recovery) prevents a single slow client or a panic from degrading the whole service, directly protecting availability and revenue.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Middleware centralizes cross-cutting concerns so business handlers stay small and testable; the single-method Handler interface makes everything mockable and composable.
foundations.performanceImpact: net/http is fast and uses one goroutine per connection/stream, scaling to high concurrency on modest hardware. The big risks are missing timeouts (resource exhaustion) and per-request allocations in hot middleware, both tunable.
commonUseCases: JSON REST APIs with a ServeMux router
Middleware chains for logging, auth, recovery, request IDs
Graceful shutdown on SIGTERM in containers

commonMisconceptions.myth: You need a framework (Gin/Echo) to build a real API.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Since Go 1.22 the standard ServeMux supports methods and path wildcards; net/http plus a little middleware is enough for most services.
By default it has NONE. A slow or malicious client can hold a connection indefinitely; you must set ReadTimeout/WriteTimeout/IdleTimeout (and ReadHeaderTimeout).

commonMisconceptions.myth: A panic in a handler only fails that request.
commonMisconceptions.reality: True only because net/http recovers per-connection by default — but it returns no useful response and logs noisily. Add your own recovery middleware to return a clean 500 and structured log.

commonMisconceptions.myth: context.WithValue is for passing optional parameters.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It's for request-scoped data that crosses API boundaries (request ID, auth principal), not for passing regular function arguments.

visualExplorer.title: Everything is an http.Handler
visualExplorer.caption: A handler is any type with ServeHTTP. HandlerFunc adapts a plain function to satisfy the interface, which is why functions, structs, and middleware all interoperate.

visualExplorer.title: A request through the middleware chain
visualExplorer.caption: How a request flows in and a response flows back out through wrapped handlers.

config.intro: Lifecycle of one request through a logging -> recovery -> auth -> handler stack:

steps.name: Accept & dispatch
steps.detail: The server accepts the connection in its own goroutine and the ServeMux matches the route to the outermost wrapped handler.

steps.name: Logging (in)
steps.detail: The outermost middleware records the start time and a request ID, then calls next.ServeHTTP.

steps.name: Recovery
steps.detail: Wraps the rest in a deferred recover() so a panic becomes a clean 500 instead of a crash.

steps.name: Auth
steps.detail: Validates the token; on failure it writes 401 and returns WITHOUT calling next, short-circuiting the chain.

steps.name: Handler & unwind
steps.detail: The business handler runs and writes the response; control unwinds back out so logging can record status and latency.

interactiveExamples.title: A middleware chain with logging, recovery, and a router
interactiveExamples.explanation: Middleware is func(http.Handler) http.Handler. We compose Recovery(Logging(mux)) so logging is outermost (sees everything) and recovery wraps the handler. The Go 1.22 mux routes by method and a path wildcard, read with r.PathValue.

interactiveExamples.title: Edit it: add a request-ID + context-aware middleware
interactiveExamples.explanation: This handler ignores cancellation and has no request ID for tracing. Edit it to inject a request ID into the context and pass r.Context() into the (simulated) downstream call so a client disconnect cancels the work.

code.expectedOutput: done (req a1b2c3d4e5f60718)   // or 499 if the client disconnects first

checkpoints.prompt: What is the type signature of idiomatic Go middleware?
checkpoints.explanation: Middleware takes the next http.Handler and returns a new http.Handler that wraps it: func(next http.Handler) http.Handler. This lets you compose chains like Recovery(Logging(Auth(mux))). The first option is a handler function, not middleware.

checkpoints.prompt: This server compiles and serves, but a single slow client can tie up a connection forever and writes after the header can panic. What's the root issue?
checkpoints.explanation: http.Server has NO default timeouts. Without ReadHeaderTimeout/ReadTimeout/WriteTimeout/IdleTimeout, a slow-loris client can hold connections open indefinitely and exhaust resources. Always set explicit timeouts on a production server.

checkpoints.prompt: Compose the chain so Logging is outermost and Recovery wraps the mux directly.
checkpoints.explanation: Wrapping is inside-out: Recovery(handler) wraps the mux first, then Logging wraps that, so the resulting Logging(Recovery(mux)) runs Logging first (outermost) on the way in. The request flows Logging -> Recovery -> mux.

checkpoints.prompt: An auth middleware writes 401 and returns WITHOUT calling next.ServeHTTP on a bad token. What does the client receive, and does the handler run?
options: 401 and the handler does NOT run (chain short-circuits)
checkpoints.explanation: By writing 401 and returning before calling next.ServeHTTP, the middleware short-circuits the chain: the protected handler never runs and the client gets only the 401. This early-return is exactly how auth/rate-limit middleware reject requests.

codeLab.title: Build a composable middleware chainer
codeLab.instructions: Implement `Chain(mws ...Middleware) Middleware` where `type Middleware func(http.Handler) http.Handler`. Chain returns a single middleware that applies them so the FIRST argument is the OUTERMOST (runs first). Then `Chain(A, B)(h)` must equal `A(B(h))`.
hints: A Middleware is func(http.Handler) http.Handler; Chain returns one of those.
To make the first argument outermost, apply the slice in REVERSE (last wraps innermost first).
Verify with Chain(A,B)(h) == A(B(h)) by checking which middleware runs first.

debuggingLab.title: 'superfluous response.WriteHeader call' in the logs
debuggingLab.symptom: Responses look fine but the server logs 'http: superfluous response.WriteHeader call' and the logged status code is always 200 even for errors.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: The first w.Write implicitly calls WriteHeader(200) because no status was set yet. The subsequent WriteHeader(400) is ignored (and logs 'superfluous'). You must call WriteHeader BEFORE writing the body. This also breaks logging middleware that captures the status after the fact — it sees 200.
commonMistakes: Writing the body before setting the status code.
Assuming a late WriteHeader changes an already-sent status.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Set the status code first (or use http.Error which does both), then write the body.

theory.question: Explain the http.Handler interface and how HandlerFunc lets a plain function serve HTTP.
theory.directAnswer: http.Handler is a one-method interface: ServeHTTP(w ResponseWriter, r *Request). The server calls ServeHTTP for each request (in its own goroutine). http.HandlerFunc is an adapter — a func(w, r) type whose own ServeHTTP method just calls the function — so you can pass an ordinary function anywhere a Handler is expected. This single-method design is what makes handlers, routers, and middleware all compose.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The universal contract for serving an HTTP request and the func adapter that satisfies it.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: A minimal interface maximizes composability — everything that handles requests shares one shape.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: HandlerFunc(f).ServeHTTP(w,r) simply calls f(w,r), bridging functions and the interface.

theory.whyImportant: It's the foundation of the entire net/http ecosystem and a near-guaranteed interview question.
theory.realWorldExample: mux.HandleFunc wraps your function in a HandlerFunc so the mux can store it as a Handler.

followUps.question: Why one goroutine per request?
followUps.answer: Goroutines are cheap, so the server handles many concurrent requests without a thread pool; handlers must still be safe for concurrent use of shared state.

followUps.question: How do you make a struct a handler?
followUps.answer: Give it a ServeHTTP method; it then satisfies http.Handler and can hold dependencies like a *sql.DB.

theory.question: What is middleware in Go, how do you order a chain, and how does a middleware short-circuit a request?
theory.directAnswer: Middleware is a func(http.Handler) http.Handler that returns a new handler wrapping the next one, adding behavior before/after next.ServeHTTP. You order them by nesting: Logging(Recovery(Auth(mux))) runs Logging first (outermost) on the way in and last on the way out. A middleware short-circuits by writing a response (e.g. 401) and returning WITHOUT calling next.ServeHTTP, so inner handlers never run.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A handler-to-handler decorator for cross-cutting concerns.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To keep logging, auth, recovery, and timeouts out of business handlers and apply them uniformly.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Each layer can run code, call next, run more code, or reject early by not calling next.

theory.whyImportant: Middleware composition is the standard way real Go services structure cross-cutting logic.
theory.realWorldExample: An auth middleware validates a JWT and either injects the user into the context and calls next, or writes 401 and returns.

followUps.question: Where should recovery sit in the chain?
followUps.answer: Outer enough to catch panics from all inner handlers but typically inside logging so the panic and resulting 500 are logged with request context.

followUps.question: How do you pass data from middleware to a handler?
followUps.answer: Attach it to the request context with r = r.WithContext(context.WithValue(...)) and read it via r.Context().Value.

scenario.question: During deploys in Kubernetes, your Go service drops in-flight requests and clients see connection resets. How do you make shutdown graceful?
scenario.directAnswer: The process is exiting on SIGTERM without draining. Catch SIGTERM, stop accepting new connections, and let in-flight requests finish with a deadline using srv.Shutdown(ctx). Concretely: run ListenAndServe in a goroutine; on signal, create a context.WithTimeout (a bit under the pod's terminationGracePeriod) and call srv.Shutdown(ctx), which closes listeners and waits for active requests to complete (or the deadline). Also flip readiness to 'not ready' first so the load balancer stops sending new traffic.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Coordinated draining of in-flight requests before process exit.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Containers receive SIGTERM before being killed; abrupt exit cuts active requests.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: srv.Shutdown stops accepting connections and blocks until handlers return or ctx times out.

scenario.whyImportant: Graceful shutdown is essential for zero-downtime deploys; getting it wrong shows up as user-visible errors during every rollout.
scenario.realWorldExample: A rolling deploy where each pod fails its readiness probe, drains for up to 25s via srv.Shutdown, then exits cleanly.

followUps.question: Why flip readiness before Shutdown?
followUps.answer: So the service is removed from the load balancer's endpoints and stops receiving new requests while it drains existing ones.

followUps.question: What if a handler hangs past the deadline?
followUps.answer: Shutdown returns context.DeadlineExceeded; you then force-exit. Per-request timeouts (and ctx propagation) prevent most hangs.

coding.question: Implement a logging middleware that records the response status code and latency. You'll need to capture the status, which ResponseWriter doesn't expose. Signature: `func Logging(next http.Handler) http.Handler`.
coding.thoughtProcess: ResponseWriter doesn't let you read back the status, so wrap it in a small struct that records the status on WriteHeader (defaulting to 200 if the handler writes a body without setting one). After calling next.ServeHTTP through the wrapper, log method, path, captured status, and elapsed time.
coding.lineByLine: statusRecorder embeds the real ResponseWriter (so it inherits Write/Header) and overrides WriteHeader to record the code. We default status to 200 because a handler that only calls Write never calls WriteHeader explicitly. We pass the recorder (not w) into next so we observe what the handler set, then log status and latency on the way out.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(1) — one small wrapper per request.

followUps.question: Why embed ResponseWriter instead of reimplementing it?
followUps.answer: Embedding promotes the existing Write/Header/Flush methods, so you only override the one method (WriteHeader) you care about.

followUps.question: How would you also capture bytes written?
followUps.answer: Override Write to add len(b) to a counter before delegating to the embedded ResponseWriter.

systemDesign.question: Design a production-ready REST API service in Go (no framework) that must be observable, resilient to bad clients, and deployable with zero downtime. Walk through the structure.
systemDesign.directAnswer: Structure it as: a configured http.Server with explicit timeouts (ReadHeaderTimeout, ReadTimeout, WriteTimeout, IdleTimeout) to defend against slow/malicious clients; a Go 1.22 ServeMux for method+path routing; and a middleware stack applied in order: RequestID -> Logging -> Recovery -> Metrics -> RateLimit -> Auth -> handler. Handlers are methods on a struct holding dependencies (DB pool, clients), keeping them testable. Every handler passes r.Context() into DB/RPC calls so client disconnects and per-request timeouts cancel downstream work. Add /healthz (liveness) and /readyz (readiness) endpoints, Prometheus /metrics, and structured logs with the request ID. For deploys: run ListenAndServe in a goroutine, on SIGTERM flip readiness off then srv.Shutdown(ctx) with a deadline to drain. Wrap downstream calls with timeouts, bounded retries, and a circuit breaker.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A standard-library HTTP service with a layered middleware stack and operational endpoints.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Production services need observability, resilience, and zero-downtime deploys around their business logic.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Server timeouts bound connections; middleware adds cross-cutting concerns uniformly; context propagation cancels work; graceful shutdown drains on SIGTERM.

systemDesign.whyImportant: It ties together every operational concern interviewers and real services care about, demonstrating you can ship, not just code.
systemDesign.realWorldExample: Kubernetes, Prometheus, and Docker all expose net/http services with exactly this shape — timeouts, middleware, health endpoints, graceful shutdown.

followUps.question: Where do you enforce per-request timeouts?
followUps.answer: Use http.TimeoutHandler or wrap r.Context() with context.WithTimeout in middleware, and propagate that context to all downstream calls.

followUps.question: How do you rate-limit fairly per client?
followUps.answer: A token-bucket limiter (golang.org/x/time/rate) keyed by API key or IP in middleware, returning 429 with a Retry-After header when exceeded.

followUps.question: How do you test handlers without a network?
followUps.answer: Use net/http/httptest: httptest.NewRequest + httptest.NewRecorder to drive ServeHTTP and assert status/body.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Keep business logic in handlers that are methods on a dependency struct (DB, clients, config) for testability. Apply cross-cutting concerns as a fixed, ordered middleware stack. Prefer the standard ServeMux (Go 1.22+) unless you need features it lacks. Expose /healthz, /readyz, and /metrics separately from business routes.
productionDeepDive.performance: net/http scales to high concurrency with one goroutine per connection/stream. Reuse a single http.Client with a tuned Transport for outbound calls (connection pooling); avoid per-request allocations in hot middleware; enable HTTP/2 and gzip where appropriate. Profile with pprof exposed on an internal-only endpoint.
productionDeepDive.concurrency: Each request runs in its own goroutine, so handlers must treat shared state as concurrent — guard caches/maps with sync primitives. Bound any fan-out a handler does (semaphore/errgroup) and always pass r.Context() downstream so cancellation propagates.
productionDeepDive.reliability: Always set server timeouts (no defaults exist). Add Recovery middleware so a panic returns a clean 500. Implement graceful shutdown (readiness flip + srv.Shutdown). Wrap downstream calls with timeouts, bounded jittered retries, and a circuit breaker to survive dependency failures.
productionDeepDive.observability: Emit structured logs with a request ID propagated via context; record RED metrics (Rate, Errors, Duration) per route with a latency histogram; integrate distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry) by extracting/injecting trace context in middleware.
productionDeepDive.security: Set ReadHeaderTimeout to defend against slow-loris; validate and size-limit request bodies (http.MaxBytesReader); set secure headers; use TLS (ListenAndServeTLS or terminate at a proxy); authenticate in middleware and authorize in handlers; never log secrets or full tokens.

caseStudies.problem: Serve many clients reliably with consistent cross-cutting behavior.
caseStudies.solution: net/http servers with layered middleware (auth, audit, metrics) and graceful shutdown.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: More boilerplate than a heavy framework, but full control and minimal dependencies.
caseStudies.lessons: The standard library plus a small middleware stack scales to enormous production systems.

caseStudies.solution: Set ReadHeaderTimeout/ReadTimeout/IdleTimeout and added per-request timeouts via context.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Aggressive timeouts can cut off legitimately slow clients; tuned per endpoint.
caseStudies.lessons: Always configure timeouts explicitly — the zero-value server is unsafe for the internet.

keyTakeaways: An HTTP service is just an http.Handler (ServeHTTP); HandlerFunc adapts plain functions, making handlers, routers, and middleware all composable.
Middleware is func(http.Handler) http.Handler; chain by nesting (outer = first in), and short-circuit by writing a response and returning without calling next.
The zero-value http.Server has NO timeouts — always set ReadHeaderTimeout/ReadTimeout/WriteTimeout/IdleTimeout and implement graceful shutdown with srv.Shutdown.
Propagate r.Context() into every downstream call so client disconnects and per-request timeouts cancel work, and add logging/recovery/metrics middleware for production observability and resilience.
